Hi Product Hunt, I'm Sen, a designer who never formally learned to code.

Over the past year I've built most of my projects by talking to Claude Code and Codex. Things got made, but I rarely saw how I actually worked with the agent: how I give direction, when I correct it, when I just let it continue.

Coding Wrapped is a small open-source Agent Skill, loosely inspired by Spotify Wrapped. It reads your local Claude Code and Codex sessions and turns them into a private dashboard on localhost:

   A few facts about your habits. For me: I used "first" in 29 messages this month, and said "continue" 14 times once a direction felt right. [...] What you did, what the agent did, and the working style that shows.

   One small suggestion per habit, drawn from a curated set of 40 practices, each with its source.

   Everything stays on your machine. Raw prompts, code, project names and secrets are not stored, and it's not a productivity score.

To try it:

> npx skills add senlindesign/coding-wrapped --skill coding-wrapped --agent claude-code --agent codex --global

Then ask your agent: "Build my Coding Wrapped."

I'd be curious to hear what it shows you.

results.content:
Zero-shot capability and token frugality don't always come from the same tool. On raw benchmark performance, Claude Opus 4.6 sits around 80.8% and GPT-5.5 powering Codex around 88.7% on the metrics one source tracked, but Claude Code holds an 88.6% SWE-bench Verified score by another measure. The benchmarks genuinely don't agree with each other depending on methodology, which is its own lesson.

Price-per-output tells a different story than raw capability. Cursor's Composer 2.5 lands in the top three on capability index while running roughly 10-60x cheaper than the leaders, so if you're optimizing purely for $/task rather than fewest tokens per task, the ranking flips entirely. [...] The efficiency numbers aren't close, and not in the direction I expected. One widely cited test had Claude Code completing an identical multi-file feature task using around 33,000 tokens with zero errors, while Cursor Agent burned roughly 188,000 tokens on the same task and hit several errors along the way, a 5.5x gap for the same deliverable. Separately, other community head-to-heads put Claude Code at roughly 3-4x the token use of Codex on comparable work, so depending which pair you're comparing, the "efficient" tool flips.
